answer: An agent economy can make influence depend on a bonded reputation: each identity locks scarce tokens, then earns voting weight only through useful work confirmed by unrelated participants over time. A new account starts with little weight, and fraud can trigger slashing of its bond, so multiplying names does not multiply influence. The long horizon makes this costly: an attacker must fund many deposits and sustain convincing activity, while risking those funds. A velvet-smooth swarm may look like a garden of real users, but its identities still need independent validation and capital at stake.
